items.question: How does this tool accurately count Unicode characters and emoji?
items.answer: We use the standard `Intl.Segmenter` API with grapheme clustering. Unlike primitive `string.length` counting which splits surrogate pairs, complex emoji sequences (such as 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 or flag emoji) are accurately counted as single visible characters.

items.question: What is the difference between characters with and without spaces?
items.answer: Characters with spaces counts every visible grapheme plus tabs, spaces, and line breaks. Characters without spaces strips all Unicode whitespace (including non-breaking spaces and line returns) before counting.

items.question: What platform limits are checked?
items.answer: The tool actively checks limits for X/Twitter (280 chars), SMS text messages (160 characters for standard GSM-7 or 70 for Unicode), SEO Meta Titles (60 chars), Meta Descriptions (160 chars), and Instagram Bios (150 chars).

items.question: Is my text transmitted or stored on your servers?
items.answer: No. All text parsing, grapheme segmentation, and keyword statistics happen entirely within your local browser sandbox. Nothing you type or paste is transmitted over the network.

items.question: How is reading and speaking time estimated?
items.answer: Reading time is computed at the standard research average of 238 words per minute. Speaking time is estimated at 150 words per minute, typical for presentations and voiceovers.

items.question: How does the word counter define a word?
items.answer: In line with Microsoft Word and Google Docs conventions, words are defined as whitespace-separated tokens containing at least one Unicode letter (\p{L}) or number (\p{N}). Hyphenated terms like "well-known" count as a single word.

items.question: Can this tool handle large documents without freezing?
items.answer: Yes. The algorithm handles multi-megabyte texts efficiently with optimized single-pass linear regex and segmenter execution.

items.question: How are sentences and paragraphs counted?
items.answer: Sentences are parsed via grammatical sentence segmenters. Paragraphs are identified as text blocks separated by one or more blank line returns.
